title: Oil Spill Spreads Along UAE Beaches Toward a Wildlife Haven
summary:
An oil spill is spreading along the coast of the United Arab Emirates, turning the water black at some beaches and worrying scientists who study sea life.

The oil is leaking from a tanker called Gem No.2. The ship was damaged on October 9 near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that many oil tankers pass through. A maritime company reported it was struck by an unknown projectile and caught fire; the fire was put out, and all 22 crew members were rescued. A small leak was spotted on October 19, and satellite images later showed the slick of oil spreading more than 35 kilometres (22 miles) from the ship.

This week, oil began washing ashore near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain, and some beaches and coastal areas were closed. The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said it “immediately began containment” to limit the damage.

Scientists say oil spills can hurt ocean animals in several ways: oil can trap sea turtles, coat the feathers of seabirds, and damage the gills of fish. The slick is also drifting toward Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a protected area of corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes that is home to green turtles and a rare fish called the Halavi guitarfish. One scientist called the spill's closeness to this special habitat the most concerning part of the story.

Experts say it is too early to know how much harm the spill will cause. That depends on how much oil leaked, how quickly it breaks down, and how well the cleanup works — which is why containing it quickly matters so much.
why_it_matters: Oil spills can damage the beaches, wildlife and waters that coastal communities depend on, and this one is drifting toward a protected habitat for turtles and a rare fish. How quickly it is contained will decide how much of that special ecosystem is harmed.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage between the Persian Gulf and the open ocean, and a large share of the world's oil travels through it aboard tanker ships.
When a tanker is damaged, oil can leak out and float on the surface, forming a slick that wind and currents push toward shore.
Floating oil is dangerous for sea life: it can trap turtles, coat the feathers of seabirds and damage the gills that fish breathe with.
Cleanup crews fight a spill by containment — trying to surround, block or collect the oil before it reaches beaches and protected habitats such as corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes.
